newsitem.title: USA: Senate to vote on "partial birth" abortion ban.
newsitem.headline: Senate to vote on "partial birth" abortion ban.

text.p: The Senate was set to vote on Tuesday on a controversial proposal to ban "partial birth" abortions, challenging U.S. President Bill Clinton to deliver his promised veto.

Buoyed by a last-minute endorsement by the influential American Medical Association, Senate sponsors of the proposed ban were scrambling to pick up five votes needed to reach 67, the number required to override a presidential veto.
The House in March passed the ban by a large margin.

A few hours before the vote, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said he could not predict the outcome, saying some senators were still "laboring" over how to vote. Among those who has publicly voiced uncertainty is Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat.
"Depending on what they decide, (it) could bring us closer to the veto override level," Lott, a Mississippi Republican, told reporters.

Clinton vetoed the bill last year and has vowed to do so again, saying it does not provide an exemption for cases in which a pregnant woman faces serious risks to her health or her ability to bear children in the future.
The bill before the Senate, sponsored by Pennsylvania Repblican Rick Santorum, allows the procedure only when it is necessary to save a woman's life.
Partial birth, also known as intact dilation and extraction, involves the partial extraction of the foetus feet-first, the subsequent suctioning out of the foetal brain and the removal of the foetus.
Should the ban be enacted, it would be the first federal restriction on an abortion procedure since the 1973 Supreme Court decision upholding a woman's right to abortion.

It is likely to face a constitutional challenge, particularly because partial birth procedures can occur in the fifth and sixth month of pregnancy, when the Supreme Court allowed less leeway for state regulation.
Sen. Bill Frist, a Tennessee Republican and the only physician in the Senate, said the health argument is a "myth."
"It's been used again and again, the president of the United States continues to use it," said Frist. "It's time to ban this procedure."
"We have a brutal, basically repulsive procedure that is specifically designed to kill a living infant outside the birth canal with only the head remaining inside," Frist said.
Sen. Barbara Boxer, a California Democrat, said several medical organisations, including the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, oppose the ban.

"This procedure is used by obstetricians and gynecologists in circumstances when they believe it is in the best interest of the woman, to save her life or save her health or save her fertility," Boxer said.
"In the opinion of the doctors, it was the humane thing to do," she added.

The Senate last week defeated two Democrat-backed alternatives that tried to change the focus away from this specific abortion procedure and instead restrict all abortions after a foetus becomes viable or able to survive outside the womb.
The measures, which had health exemptions, failed but Lott and other Republicans said they might eventually be the basis for future legislation.
